meta.title: RLHF, DPO, and Preference Tuning
meta.thesis: RLHF and DPO use preference signals after pretraining to steer model behavior: RLHF trains a reward model and optimizes a policy, while DPO trains directly on chosen/rejected pairs.

mentalMap.title: Preference tuning — chosen beats rejected
mentalMap.caption: The map separates preference data, RLHF’s reward-model path, DPO’s offline path, and failure modes.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: Preference tuning teaches models from comparisons when “better” is easier to rank than to write as one perfect answer.

modules.title: When gold answers are too narrow
modules.sub: Start with why comparisons are useful after supervised behavior exists.
modules.summary: Many assistant qualities are easier to rank than to specify as one canonical response.
objectives: Avoid using preferences for missing facts.

blocks.title: Better is sometimes easier than exact

spans.text: For many assistant behaviors, there is no single perfect target answer. Reviewers can still prefer one answer over another: safer, less verbose, more honest about uncertainty, or better at asking a clarifying question.
Preference tuning exists for that layer. It should come after the model already knows the task format; it steers quality, judgment, and style.

blocks.analogy: Preference tuning is like coaching from comparisons: “do more like this answer, less like that one.”

spans.text: Prompt: “Can I get reimbursed?” Chosen response asks which policy and date apply. Rejected response invents a universal reimbursement rule. The preferred answer is not longer or flashier; it is safer behavior.

blocks.title: Check purpose

options.text: When the app needs the latest policy facts.
When reviewers can reliably rank outputs for qualities like helpfulness or safety.
When no evals or examples exist yet.

blocks.explanation: Preference tuning needs meaningful comparisons and held-out checks.

modules.title: Preference pairs are the data unit
modules.sub: Before algorithms, inspect the chosen/rejected examples.
modules.summary: The quality of prompts, chosen responses, rejected responses, and label instructions determines what the model learns.

blocks.title: A pair must isolate the behavior you want

spans.text: A preference pair usually contains a prompt, a chosen response, and a rejected response. If the chosen answer differs in tone, length, factuality, and safety all at once, the model may learn the wrong feature.
Good pairs are comparable. They make the desired preference clear: cite uncertainty, refuse unsafe action, ask a clarifying question, or follow the tool policy.

blocks.analogy: A preference pair is like two drafts with one deliberate difference for the editor to choose between.

blocks.title: Inspect a tiny preference pair

spans.text: Run this as a tiny model of the mechanism. The point is to predict behavior before trusting the output.

predictThenReveal.answer: It prints asks_for_required_info. The pair teaches the model to request required information instead of taking an unsupported action.

syntax.explains: The small concrete case the example operates on.
The line or function that turns the inputs into behavior.
A visible result so you can check your prediction.

options.text: The rejected answer is not exactly the same length.
Chosen and rejected differ in many uncontrolled ways, so the learned preference is ambiguous.

modules.title: RLHF: reward model then policy update
modules.sub: With preference data understood, open the more complex training route.
modules.summary: RLHF trains a reward model from rankings, then optimizes a policy model while constraining drift from a reference.
objectives: Explain why KL or reference control matters.

blocks.title: RLHF adds a learned reward layer

spans.text: In the RLHF recipe, reviewers rank outputs. A reward model learns to score outputs from those rankings. The policy model is then optimized to increase reward while staying close to a reference model.
The extra machinery is useful when on-policy optimization matters, but it creates extra failure modes: reward hacking, instability, and over-optimization.

blocks.analogy: RLHF is like training a judge, then training a performer to please that judge without drifting too far from the original act.

spans.text: A reward model overvalues refusals because labelers preferred safe answers. The policy learns to refuse harmless requests. The win rate improves on safety pairs but factual usefulness drops.
The fix is not just a lower learning rate. The team needs balanced preference data and held-out evals for helpfulness, factuality, and safe completion.

blocks.title: Check RLHF
blocks.prompt: What is a reward model used for?

options.text: Scoring candidate responses based on learned preferences.

blocks.explanation: The reward model maps outputs to preference-like scores used during optimization.

modules.title: DPO: optimize the pair directly
modules.sub: Compare the simpler offline route after RLHF.
modules.summary: DPO trains the policy to prefer chosen responses over rejected responses directly from static pairs, without a separate reward model.
objectives: Explain DPO at a high level.
Know when DPO is a good fit.

blocks.title: DPO removes the separate reward model

spans.text: Direct Preference Optimization uses chosen/rejected pairs to train the policy so it assigns higher relative likelihood to the chosen response. It avoids a separate reward model and online reinforcement-learning loop.
DPO is attractive when you already have high-quality static preference pairs and want a simpler training pipeline. It still inherits all the risks of the data.

blocks.analogy: DPO is like training directly from edited pairs instead of first training a separate critic.

blocks.title: RLHF vs DPO in a team decision

spans.text: A lab with infrastructure for online sampling and reward modeling may choose RLHF for complex reward shaping. A product team with 20,000 carefully reviewed chosen/rejected support answers may choose DPO for a simpler offline run.
The decision turns less on hype and more on data quality, infrastructure, and eval coverage.

blocks.title: Check DPO

options.text: A separate reward model and online RL loop.

blocks.explanation: DPO simplifies training mechanics but does not eliminate data and eval requirements.

modules.title: Preference gains can hide regressions
modules.sub: End with the advanced failure modes that decide ship/no-ship.
modules.summary: Preference tuning can improve ranked style while hurting factuality, tool use, diversity, or long-context behavior.
objectives: Choose what to monitor after tuning.

spans.text: Preference data encodes labeler values and blind spots. A tuned model can become more pleasing while becoming less factual, less diverse, too cautious, or worse at tool use.

items.text: Reward hacking: outputs exploit the judge rather than improve usefulness.
Over-caution: the model refuses safe requests.
Confounded preferences: the model learns length or tone instead of correctness.
Distribution shift: held-out traffic differs from labeled pairs.

spans.text: When an AI proposes RLHF or DPO, demand evidence of a real training plan.

items.text: Does it define the source and audit process for preference pairs?
Does it compare RLHF and DPO rather than naming one by default?
Does it include factuality, safety, and tool-use regression evals?
Does it specify a reference model and rollback path?

blocks.title: Check failure modes
blocks.prompt: What is the biggest warning sign before shipping a preference-tuned model?

options.text: The dataset contains chosen and rejected answers.
Preference win rate improves while factuality or safety regressions are unmeasured.
The team chose DPO over RLHF.

blocks.explanation: Preference metrics must be paired with regression evals.
